title: High-throughput synthesis of DNA fragments by molecular self-assembly of overlapping oligonucleotides - Nature Biotechnology
text:
AbstractThe limitations of DNA synthesis technologies are a fundamental bottleneck in synthetic biology. Here we present a high-throughput gene synthesis method driven by hybridization, called Molecular Self-Assembly Induced Cloning. Molecular Self-Assembly Induced Cloning overcomes molecular crosstalk and oligo misalignment across genes by coupling orthogonal self-assembly of overlapping DNA segments in vitro with the DNA repair machineries of host cells in vivo. Cellular uptake of the assembled target fragments serves as templates for recovery and cloning. We adopt microchip-based oligonucleotide synthesis, enabling the production of over 1,000 distinct gene fragments in a simple one-pot reaction. Near-zero misalignment is an indispensable feature of the parallel synthesis, with oligo synthesis errors remaining at a constant but controllable level. We also construct massive variant libraries of the industrial enzyme PETase and discover higher-potency variants than the gold standard enzyme.

Additional informationPublisher’s note Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations.Extended dataExtended Data Fig. 1 Nicking endonuclease-based recombination.To facilitate recombination, two nicking endonuclease cutting sites were digested at the vector ends, generating short, non-continuous strands. Simultaneously, the gene fragment ends were extended using longer oligonucleotides, which readily generated two overhangs. These overhangs on the assembled fragment could then displace the shorter strands and complement the vector, thereby forming a circular double-stranded DNA. We transformed this product into E. coli, where the nicks would be repaired in vivo. This method was utilized for the recombination of all fragments with the vector in this paper, except for two combinatorial libraries, which were recombined using the ClonExpress Ultra One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme) to prevent the insertion of the overhang sequence.Extended Data Fig. 2 Schematic for segmentation.We padded the original 720 bp gfp gene fragment to 810 bp with functional ends at first. The bases are indexed from 1 to 810 in the 5′ to 3′ direction. The first forward oligo, F1, spans bases 31 to 90, F2 spans bases 91 to 150, and so forth, concluding with F13, which spans bases 751 to 810. This segmentation pattern is mirrored on the reverse complementary strand. Consequently, the segmentation of this padded fragment yielded 26 60-mers oligonucleotides, each complementary to the designated domains of its neighboring strands. Furthermore, the F-tail and R-tail oligos are 45-mers comprising a 15-nt overhang (represented by the green and red lines) and a 30-nt domain complementary to the target fragment. In this specific design shown in figure, the offsets are positioned at the 5′ end (with segmentation starting at base +30), resulting in 5′ overhangs. However, the assembly design is flexible: if desired by the user, the offset can alternatively be configured at the 3′ end, which would correspondingly shift the overhangs to the 3′ termini.Extended Data Fig. 3 Investigating the maximum length of single fragment synthesizable by MOSAIC.a, We tested the assembly of fragments ranging from 300 bp up to 3,000 bp. Lanes 1 to 10 were loaded with fragments of increasing sizes: 300 bp, 600 bp, 900 bp, 1200 bp, 1500 bp, 1800 bp, 2100 bp, 2400 bp, 2700 bp and 3000 bp. Even the 3,000 bp assembly product displayed a distinct band on the gel, indicating successful assembly across this size range. Gel band of assembly product in lane 3 consistently appeared in a low yield from multiple rounds of repetitive experments. As experiments with a newly ordered batch yielded a band intensity comparable to those in the other lanes (data not shown), we attribute the yield difference to batch variation of oligo quality. b, The maximum assembled fragment size reached 9.9 kb, though it yielded only a indistinct band on the gel. c, We conducted a series of experiments to determine the upper limit of the recombination method. When directly recombined with the vector, the assembled fragment containing 40 nicks yielded viable clones. Given that our oligo length is 60 nt, 40 nicks correspond to a 1,200 bp fragment. When T4 ligase was applied to the ligation process, up to a 3 kb fragment yielded viable clones with the correct sequence verified by Sanger sequencing. d, Analysis of the length distribution of human coding sequence (CDS) revealed that the majority of human genes range between 600 bp and 2,000 bp. Furthermore, choosing 3000 bp as the cut-off point ensures coverage of more than 88% of all human genes.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 4 Assembly of 100% AT fragment and PCA controls of synthesis tasks 1–3.a, The gel result for the 100% AT fragment assembly showed a target band at the correct position, confirming successful assembly of the AT-rich sequence. b, Despite our efforts in optimizing the reaction conditions, all four constructs failed in PCA with no target band displayed. We attribute the failure of the secondary structure and 100% AT/CG groups to unintended base pairing. The failure of the repetitive group likely results from nonspecific extension from PCA intermediate products. The reannealed PCA intermediates with offset overhangs can extend to increasing lengths round by round, thereby generating products of indefinite lengths.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 5 Direct assembly of plasmids of different lengths.a, Schematic illustration of the two-step assembly strategy and the mini-plasmid. The component oligos required for one full-length plasmid were divided into two pools. Each pool self-assembles to form a 600 bp half-plasmid, and equimolar amounts of the two half-plasmids are then mixed to assemble the 1.2 kb full-length mini-plasmid. Both one-pot assembly and two-step assembly were tested. For the two-step assembly, both oligo pools were loaded onto the same gel (left). The two recovered half-plasmids were subsequently mixed for annealing, and the annealed product was loaded onto the gel again (right). For the one-pot assembly, all strands were mixed together and loaded onto the gel (right). Although the one-pot lane exhibited substantial smearing, the content corresponding to the position designated by the two-step lane was excised, recovered, and transformed into E. coli. b, Agarose gel image of the assembled half-mini-plasmid + gfp products. The gel displays the half-mini-plasmid + gfp 1, half-mini-plasmid + gfp 2, and the two half-pUC19 fragments (half-pUC19 1 and half-pUC19 2). c, Agarose gel image of the assembled half-3.3kb-plasmid products. d, Assembly efficiency of the 3.3 kb plasmid demonstrated in yeast. Clones from selective plates were randomly picked for PCR analysis using five specific primer pairs (top left). Clones exhibiting the designated PCR amplicons (bottom, exemplary gel result) were considered successfully assembled. Three independent rounds of experiments, each verifying eight clones, confirmed that all tested plasmids were properly assembled. Enzymatic digestion and Sanger sequencing results of plasmids isolated from two representative yeast clones are also shown (right). e, Agarose gel image of the assembled third-9.9kb-plasmid products.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 6 Two rounds of sequencing and the distribution of error-free read counts for the 92 genes.a, With an initial round of sequencing of 2,050 isolated clones based on the assembly product, we observed error-free sequences for 76 genes, and 93 genes have at least one synthetic fragment within five mutations. Then, a specific correlation between clone’s position on a plate and gene it contained was established via an in-situ PCR workflow as described in Supplementary Fig. 7. By sequencing just 200 additional targeted clones (selectively sequence the genes that are absent before), we achieved a combined recovery of 92 error-free genes and 97 genes within five mutations in total. b, The distribution of the error-free counts of 94 genes. Several genes were more likely to yield survived clones on the plate, but the overall distribution is not overly skewed.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 7 Construction of FP library and identification of new variants.a, Design schematic of the degenerate primers targeting selected sites. The corresponding DNA sequences and the possibilities for amino acid substitutions are listed. b, NGS result showing the even distribution of the library variants. Out of 1.4 million sequencing reads, approximately 564,000 contained amino acid sequences belonging to the predicted library. The appearance frequency of most individual variants was less than five times per read, which indicates an even distribution of the library complexity. c, Initial screening of the small E. coli library (approximately 800 clones) performed using a stereoscopic fluorescence microscope. d, Amino acid sequences of the newly identified fluorescent proteins (FPs). Mutations in the control FPs (Emerald, Topaz, and EBFP) are highlighted in green, orange, and blue, respectively. The mutations found in the newly identified FPs differ substantially from those in the controls, with combinations that have not been previously reported. e, Fluorescence detection of bacterial cells using a confocal microscope. All newly identified variants exhibited reasonable fluorescence at the single-cell level. NC: Negative Control (pUC19 empty vector). f, Fluorescence intensity of E. coli clones containing Y1, Y2, G2, and G4, measured using the FITC channel of a flow cytometer. NC: Negative Control (pUC19 empty vector). g-h, Fluorescence intensity of E. coli clones containing Y1, Y2, G2, and G4, measured using a plate reader. n = 3 independent colonies. The error bars indicate SD. Y1 and Y2 demonstrated brightness enhancements of 13.6-fold and 6.6-fold, respectively, compared to the Topaz control. G2 and G4 demonstrated 7.9-fold and 17.1-fold stronger bacterial fluorescence, respectively, compared to the Emerald control. The mean fluorescence intensity of the controls was normalized to 1. i, Fluorescence detection of bacterial cells using the PB450 channel of the flow cytometer. The gel result of the crude cell extract (top gel) reveals that the fluorescence enhancement observed in Y1 and Y2 may be partially attributed to a higher expression level. Following purification and concentration standardization (bottom gel), G2 and G4 still showed higher specific intensity than control (Fig. 4d).Source dataExtended Data Fig. 8 Construction of PETase library and identification of new variants.a, The amino acid possibilities at all selected sites are listed, resulting in a theoretical combinatorial library size of 43 million variants. b, NGS results revealed an even distribution of the library variants. Out of approximately 11 M sequencing reads, around 1 M reads contained amino acid sequences belonging to the predicted library and be defined as valid reads. Crucially, almost all individual variants appeared less than three reads, which indicates a high and even complexity of the library. c, Wild-type (WT) PETase was induced for protein expression and subsequently incubated with the substrate FDBz for one hour. After centrifugation, the bacteria were resuspended in fresh LB medium. Since green fluorescence was clearly observed in the WT strain but not in the negative control, we confirmed that FDBz was successfully taken up by the cell and subsequently degraded by the intracellular PETase. d, The amino acid sequences of the different variants are presented. The mutations in each variant were observed to be highly divergent (or, substantially distinct). e, All seven variants were induced for expression and purified. After purification and concentration standardization, the enzymatic performance was assessed. f, V1 demonstrated the highest enzymatic performance, with V2 to V4 also exhibiting comparable activity to the P1 and P2 controls. n = 3 independent purified proteins. The error bars indicate SD.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 9 Comparison of mismatch tolerance between PCA and MOSAIC.a, Schematics. DNA oligos, towards two target fragments containing a humongous region (as shown in gray), were subjected to one-pot PCA or MOSAIC reaction. For the two sets of oligos, we designed a 30-bp homologous region, within which a short segment (1-, 3- or 5-bp; 0-bp as a control for the 30-bp to be 100% homologous) of different sequences. Therefore, correctly aligned assembly would lead to products of X1×2 (330 bp) and Y1Y2 (570 bp); misaligned assembly would lead to byproducts of X1Y2 (450 bp) and Y1X2 (450 bp). b, Native agarose gel analysis of assembly products. In MOSAIC method, only correctly aligned products (showing only target products of a kb and b kb) were properly generated with extreme homology down to 1-bp difference. In contrast, PCA led to both correctly aligned and misaligned products for all the samples with 1-, 3- or 5-bp difference for homologous region.Source dataExtended Data Fig. 10 Misalignment prevention.a, When a large number of oligos for multiple genes are mixed, oilgos of high homology are inevitable. Therefore, the mismatching events can lead to mispriming and the error becomes irreversible in PCA. b, The same mismatching events also occurs in MOSAIC, but they can be corrected by strand displacement because hybridization reactions are reversible. c, Mismatching tends to happen for oilgos with high GC-contents and strong secondary structures as kinetic traps.
